Lesser foam frog (Leptodactylus latrans) is a large-bodied neotropical anuran that exhibits substantial sexual size dimorphism. Field surveys in the Brazilian Cerrado indicate that newly metamorphosed juveniles emerge from aquatic habitats at a snout-vent length of approximately 1.98 centimeters , a size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves provisioned during embryonic development. This initial body size is derived from eggs measuring roughly 3 millimeters in diameter, which yield a wet weight at birth of only 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], placing this species among the heavier anuran neonates for its reproductive mode. Following metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic froglets undertake a period of rapid somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity, a transition that is tightly linked to both resource availability and thermal conditions experienced during early development.

The timing of metamorphosis in Leptodactylus latrans has been examined under controlled laboratory conditions to disentangle temperature-dependent developmental rates from genetic variation. When tadpoles were reared at a constant water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], metamorphic climax was reached after 45 days , a relatively short larval period compared to many other neotropical foam-nesting frogs. This rapid development likely reflects selection for pond desiccation avoidance in ephemeral breeding habitats, where accelerated metamorphosis conveys a clear survival advantage. The age at which these newly metamorphosed animals first begin exogenous feeding and growth as terrestrial juveniles is critical for understanding their life-history scheduling, as it sets the stage for subsequent maturation and eventual reproduction.

Reproductive maturation in this species proceeds gradually, with individuals attaining puberty at a snout-vent length of roughly 6.2 centimeters [Lp = roughly 6.2 centimeters] and a corresponding body mass of about 33 grams [Wwp = about 33 grams], signaling the onset of gonadal activity. Under the same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], first reproduction in the wild is typically observed at 365 days following metamorphosis [tR = 365 days following metamorphosis], a milestone that aligns with the onset of the rainy season when ephemeral ponds become available for foam-nest construction. This relatively early age at first breeding, compared to longer-lived ranids, emphasizes a life-history strategy favoring early reproductive output over extended somatic growth, consistent with the species' occupancy of unpredictable aquatic environments.

Adult male lesser foam frogs achieve a maximum recorded snout-vent length of 12 centimeters [Li = 12 centimeters], whereas females, although slightly smaller in linear dimensions, attain an ultimate SVL of 10.6 centimeters [Li = 10.6 centimeters] and a maximum wet body mass of 147.15 grams [Wwi = 147.15 grams]. Despite their shorter length, the females exhibit a pronounced reproductive investment, and the males, interestingly, reach a substantially higher ultimate wet weight of 202.55 grams [Wwi = 202.55 grams] due to their more robust body proportions and greater musculature associated with territorial defense. These size parameters, derived from long-term mark-recapture studies, are among the largest recorded for any member of the Leptodactylus genus and suggest a relatively slow growth trajectory following the onset of breeding activities, with individuals allocating substantial resources to maintenance rather than continued somatic expansion.

Longevity records for Leptodactylus latrans, compiled from a captive colony maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], indicate that the oldest documented individual survived for 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], a lifespan that is moderate among South American leptodactylids but notably longer than that of smaller congeners. The maximum reproductive rate for this species, estimated from foam-nest production under optimal conditions at the same temperature, is approximately 7 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 7 clutches per year] during the peak rainy season, a value derived from long-term field observations of nesting female activity.
